text: Running an architecture review. Lesson nine covered writing a design document well. This lesson covers the meeting that document is usually written for — the architecture review itself. Running one well is a distinct skill from writing a good document, because a strong document can still produce a bad review if the meeting isn't structured to actually reach a decision.

A review that ends with 'great, thanks everyone, lots to think about' has failed, even if everyone found it interesting. The point was never to inform people — it was to reach one of three concrete outcomes: approved, approved with specific changes, or rejected with specific reasons. If the room disperses without landing on one of those, the review didn't do its job.

A structure that reliably gets there has four steps. State the decision being asked for, explicitly, at the start. Walk through the design doc's structure — problem, design, alternatives, risks — not a line-by-line re-read. Explicitly invite objections before asking for approval. And name the decision out loud at the end, with any conditions attached.

A common disruption is a reviewer raising a real concern that's genuinely outside what this document was trying to decide. The skill is acknowledging it's real without letting it hijack the meeting: 'that's legitimate, and it's outside today's scope — let's capture it as a follow-up and keep moving on today's actual decision.'

'We'll take it offline' can be the right call, or an avoidance tactic. The honest test: does the main decision still get made in this meeting, with only a narrow sub-question deferred? If yes, deferring that piece was correct. If the entire decision gets deferred under this phrase, the review just postponed having to do its job.

Running a review well means leaving with an actual decision, every time. Next up, lesson thirteen: mentoring through a hard technical problem — where the shift from answering to shaping gets tested one on one.
